lead: This unit explains the aircraft systems that move the surfaces, feed air and fuel, keep the cabin breathable and put out fires. After it you can trace hydraulic and pneumatic power from source to user, size a brake or an oxygen bottle, describe a pressurisation and cooling pack, and explain how fire, stall, ice and rain are detected and handled.
about: Unit 2 covers the aircraft systems that keep the aircraft flying, breathing and stopping. Chapter 2.1 starts with hydraulic power, its components and its modes; 2.2 follows bleed air, the source of pneumatic power; 2.3 uses both for landing gear and brakes. Chapters 2.4 and 2.5 go inside the engine for fuel, oil, starting and ignition. Chapters 2.6 and 2.7 handle the cabin: pressurisation, air cycle cooling, vapour cycle cooling and heating; 2.8 covers oxygen when pressurisation fails. Chapter 2.9 covers fire and smoke detection and extinguishing, 2.10 links gear and flap control with stall warning and protection, and 2.11 closes with ice and rain protection.

chapters.idea: A hydraulic system stores and delivers pressurised fluid to actuators, and its controllers choose which supply path and which mode the aircraft uses.
chapters.depth: Pascal's law and F = p × A; typical transport pressure 3000 psi (about 207 bar); open-centre and closed-centre systems; reservoir, filter, engine-driven pump, electric pump, hand pump, accumulator with nitrogen precharge, relief valve, selector valve, servo valve, actuator, hydraulic fuse. Pump controllers and the normal, alternate and emergency modes. Some syllabi call the accumulator an oil-gas accumulator. Keep the mode table short.

figure.title: Hydraulic supply to a user
figure.aria: Fluid leaves the reservoir, is pressurised by the pumps, stored briefly in the accumulator, routed by a selector valve to an actuator and returned to the reservoir.

chapters.example: An actuator piston has diameter 5 cm and the system supplies 207 bar. Area = π × (0.025 m)² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m². Pressure = 207 × 10⁵ Pa. Extension force = p × A = 40 640 N ≈ 40.6 kN. The rod side has rod diameter 2 cm, so annulus area = 1.963 × 10⁻³ − 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.649 × 10⁻³ m² and retraction force = 34.1 kN.
chapters.trap: Treating the accumulator's nitrogen precharge as the working pressure, and mixing 3000 psi with 3000 kPa.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for what the actuators move.
chapters.leave: Electrical generation for the pumps to Unit 3; fly-by-wire signalling to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Bleed air taken from the engine compressor is regulated through a manifold and then feeds air conditioning, pressurisation, anti-icing and engine starting.
chapters.depth: Sources: high-pressure and low-pressure compressor bleed, APU, ground cart. Pressure regulating and shut-off valve, precooler, manifold with check and isolation valves, overpressure and overheat protection, temperature and pressure sensors, list of users. Give only ranges: a few hundred kPa and a few hundred degrees Celsius before cooling. Some syllabi call this the typical air pressure system.

figure.title: Typical air pressure system
figure.aria: Engine and APU bleed pass through a precooler and a pressure regulating valve into an isolated manifold that supplies the air conditioning packs, anti-ice and engine start.

chapters.example: A bleed duct carries 0.3 kg/s of air at 250 kPa and 200 °C through an area of 0.01 m². Take R = 287 J/(kg·K) and T = 473 K. Density ρ = p/(RT) = 250 000/(287 × 473) = 1.84 kg/m³. Velocity v = mass flow/(ρ × A) = 0.3/(1.84 × 0.01) = 16.3 m/s.
chapters.trap: Assuming bleed air is always available: at low engine power only the high-pressure stage can supply it, and the HP valve closes again at high power.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for how pumps and valves are driven.
chapters.leave: Cooling and pressurisation to 2.6 and 2.7; engine start to 2.5; wing heat to 2.11.

chapters.idea: Landing gear carries the aircraft on the ground through an oleo shock absorber, and the brakes turn kinetic energy into heat to stop it.
chapters.depth: Classification: fixed or retractable, nose wheel or tail wheel, single or multiple wheel, bogie. Oleo strut: gas spring and oil damper, static and dynamic seals. Retraction mechanism: actuators, uplocks, downlocks, sequence and squat switch. Wheels, tyres, tyre pressures. Brakes: single and multi-disc, carbon-carbon, hydraulic actuation, antiskid with wheel speed sensors, autobrake, parking brake, brake energy and brake temperature. Some syllabi list a rocket separation mechanism under this heading; give it one line as stage separation on a booster.

figure.aria: The tree sorts landing gear into fixed and retractable layouts, with main gear as single wheel or bogie, and lists the oleo strut and the brake types beside them.

chapters.example: A 60 000 kg aircraft touches down at 250 km/h (69.4 m/s). Kinetic energy = ½ × 60 000 × 69.4² = 145 MJ. If 60 % is absorbed by the four main-wheel brakes, each brake takes 0.6 × 145/4 = 21.7 MJ. Carbon brakes are chosen because they survive this heat and stay light.
chapters.trap: Swapping the oleo roles (nitrogen is the spring, oil is the damper) and forgetting that brake energy rises with the square of landing speed.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for retraction and brake hydraulic pressure.
chapters.leave: Antiskid electronics and gear position indication to Unit 3; gear and flap control logic to 2.10.

chapters.idea: The fuel system meters the right fuel flow to the combustor, and the oil system removes heat and wear debris from the bearings.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this unit in detail; keep it short. Fuel: tanks, boost pump, low-pressure and high-pressure pumps, fuel-oil heat exchanger, filter, metering unit or FADEC, flow meter, refuel and jettison. Oil: dry-sump versus wet-sump, tank, pressure and scavenge pumps, filter with bypass, cooler, chip detector, pressure and temperature limits.

figure.title: Fuel path to the combustor
figure.aria: Fuel moves from the tank through a boost pump and a fuel-oil heat exchanger to the high-pressure pump, then is metered and sprayed through the nozzles.

chapters.example: An engine burns 1200 kg/h of fuel of density 0.8 kg/L. Volume flow = 1200/0.8 = 1500 L/h = 25 L/min = 0.42 L/s. On the oil side, 0.5 kg/s of oil with specific heat 2.0 kJ/(kg·K) picks up 60 kW: temperature rise = 60/(0.5 × 2.0) = 60 K.
chapters.trap: Treating the low-pressure and high-pressure pumps as interchangeable, and forgetting that the filter bypass lets unfiltered oil reach the bearings.
chapters.leave: Fuel quantity indication to Unit 3; FADEC scheduling laws to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The starter spins the engine to a self-sustaining speed, then the ignition system lights the fuel and combustion takes over.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; write it shorter. Air turbine starter and start valve, electric starter and starter-generator, ignition exciters and igniter plugs, low-energy and high-energy ignition, continuous ignition in rain or turbulence, start sequence and interlocks, hot start, hung start, dry motoring, APU and cross-bleed starts.

figure.aria: The starter cranks from 0 to 20 s, igniters come on at 15 s, fuel at 17 s, light-off near 19 s and the engine reaches idle by about 40 s.

chapters.example: A start takes 40 s to reach 60 % N2. Average acceleration = 60/40 = 1.5 % N2 per second. The starter cuts out at 20 s, when N2 is about 25 %, which must be above the self-sustaining speed for the ignition to keep the engine running.
chapters.trap: Switching ignition on before enough N2 gives a hot start, and starter cut-out is scheduled on N2, not on a fixed clock.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for air starts and chapter 4 for the fuel that must be lit.
chapters.leave: Starter-generator wiring to Unit 3; FADEC start scheduling to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The cabin is held at a safe pressure altitude by an outflow valve, while air cycle machines cool bleed air by expanding it through a turbine.
chapters.depth: Need for pressurisation: hypoxia, gas expansion in the body, cabin altitude limit near 8000 ft, maximum differential pressure. Outflow valve, cabin pressure controller, positive and negative relief valves, modes for ground, takeoff, climb, cruise and descent. Air cycle cooling: simple and bootstrap, flow control valve, primary and secondary heat exchangers, compressor, turbine, water separator, ram air, temperature control valve. Explain why expansion cools without cycle mathematics.

figure.title: Air cycle pack
figure.aria: Bleed air is metered, cooled in two heat exchangers, compressed in between, then cooled sharply by expansion in the turbine before water is removed and the air enters the cabin.

chapters.example: The cabin is held at 8000 ft, where pressure is 75.6 kPa, while the aircraft flies at 35 000 ft, where pressure is 23.8 kPa. Differential pressure = 75.6 − 23.8 = 51.8 kPa (about 7.5 psi). On a door of area 1.2 m² the outward load is F = p × A = 51 800 × 1.2 = 62.2 kN.
chapters.trap: Thinking the pack's compressor cools the air; it heats it. The turbine cools. Pressure is set by the outflow valve, not by the supply.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for the bleed air source.
chapters.leave: Oxygen after a depressurisation to 2.8; pack control electronics to Unit 3 or Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A vapour cycle machine cools by evaporating and condensing a refrigerant, and cabin heating adds heat from electric elements or hot bleed air.
chapters.depth: Vapour compression cycle and its four steps; compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator; coefficient of performance COP = heat absorbed/compressor work; refrigerants such as R-134a. Advantages: works on the ground without ram air, higher COP than an air cycle at low altitude. Disadvantages: weight, refrigerant handling, leakage. Cabin heating: need, electric heaters, bleed-air trim with a mixing valve, exhaust muff heat for small aircraft, foot and windshield heat.

figure.title: Vapour cycle loop
figure.aria: Refrigerant is compressed, gives up heat in the condenser, is throttled by the expansion valve, absorbs heat in the evaporator and returns to the compressor.

chapters.example: The evaporator absorbs 12 kW from the cabin and the compressor shaft takes 3 kW. COP = 12/3 = 4. Heat rejected at the condenser = 12 + 3 = 15 kW, which is why the condenser needs a good ram air flow.
chapters.trap: Mixing up condenser and evaporator, and believing COP above 1 breaks the first law: the extra heat is the compressor work.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6 for the air cycle comparison and chapter 2 for the air supply.
chapters.leave: Refrigerant chemistry and electrical loads to other units and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Above a safe cabin altitude, stored or chemical oxygen raises the partial pressure of oxygen reaching the lungs.
chapters.depth: Need: hypoxia and time of useful consciousness, which falls to tens of seconds at very high cabin altitude. Types: high-pressure gaseous (cylinder near 1800 psi), liquid oxygen, chemical generator (sodium chlorate candle), on-board oxygen generating system for military aircraft. Components: cylinder, filler valve, shut-off valve, regulator (demand, diluter-demand, pressure-demand), mask, tubing, pressure gauge. Crew and passenger systems, automatic mask drop-out. Advantages and limits of each type.

figure.aria: The tree divides oxygen supply into stored high-pressure gas with its crew, passenger and portable branches, liquid oxygen, chemical generators and military on-board generation.

chapters.example: A cylinder of 50 L water volume is filled to 124 bar. Gas available at 1 bar = 50 × 124 = 6200 L. Twelve passengers on masks at 4 L/min each need 48 L/min, so the supply lasts 6200/48 = 129 min, about 2 hours.
chapters.trap: Reading cylinder pressure as quantity, and forgetting that oxygen makes grease and oil burn fiercely.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6 for why pressurisation can fail.
chapters.leave: Mask microphones and cockpit indication to Units 3 and 4.

chapters.idea: Fire and smoke detectors watch the engine, APU, cargo and toilet zones and trigger a warning followed by a one-shot extinguisher discharge.
chapters.depth: Requirements: fast response, low false alarms, full zone coverage, testable, resettable after test. Detection: thermocouple, bimetallic spot detector, continuous loop (Kidde and Fenwal), ultraviolet and infrared flame detectors, ionisation and optical smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors. Control unit and test switch. Extinguishing: engine and APU bottles, two-shot discharge, cargo bottles, lavatory bottle, portable extinguishers, fire handle, squibs. Agents: Halon 1301 and its replacements, water mist, dry powder, carbon dioxide.

figure.title: From detection to discharge
figure.aria: A detector loop signals the control unit, which raises a cockpit warning; the pilot pulls the fire handle, the squib fires and the bottle discharges agent into the zone.

chapters.example: A cargo compartment of 40 m³ needs 6 % agent by volume. Agent volume = 0.06 × 40 = 2.4 m³. With an agent vapour density of about 6 kg/m³, the mass needed is 2.4 × 6 = 14.4 kg of agent in the bottle.
chapters.trap: Confusing smoke detection in the cargo hold with fire suppression, and forgetting the loop must be tested before flight.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5 for the engine zones that are protected.
chapters.leave: Loop wiring to Unit 3; warning display formats to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Gear and flap positions are sequenced and locked by control logic, and stall warning warns the crew while stall protection acts on the aircraft.
chapters.depth: Gear control: selector, actuation, uplock and downlock, position indication, warning when gear is up with low power, squat switch, alternate extension. Flap control: trailing edge Fowler flaps, selector, asymmetry and skew detection, limit switches, load limiting. Stall: angle of attack vane, stall warning computer, stick shaker, warning horn, stick pusher, angle of attack limit and autothrottle alpha floor. Gear hydraulics stay in chapter 3.

figure.title: Stall warning and protection
figure.aria: Angle of attack, flap position and air data feed the stall computer, which drives the stick shaker as a warning and the stick pusher as protection.

chapters.example: An aircraft stalls at 120 kt at mass 50 000 kg. Stall speed varies as 1/√mass, so at 40 000 kg it is 120 × √(40/50) = 120 × 0.894 = 107 kt. Setting the warning at 1.15 times stall speed gives 107 × 1.15 = 123 kt.
chapters.trap: Reversing shaker and pusher, and forgetting the gear warning depends on power setting as well as gear position.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 for the gear, Unit 1 for the flight controls and Unit 3 for air data.
chapters.leave: Fly-by-wire protection laws to Unit 1; airspeed indicator internals to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Ice destroys lift and blocks sensors, so critical areas are kept clear by heat, fluid or mechanical removal, and rain is cleared from the windscreen.
chapters.depth: Need: ice weight, rough leading edge, earlier stall, pitot and static blockage, engine and propeller ice. Anti-icing prevents ice; de-icing removes ice after it forms. Types: thermal bleed air, electro-thermal, chemical weeping wing and freeze-point depressant, pneumatic boots, electro-expulsive. Areas: wing and tail leading edges, engine inlet, propeller, windshield, pitot and static heads, drain masts. Rain removal: wipers, rain repellent, hot air. Ice detection methods.

figure.aria: The tree sorts ice protection into thermal methods using bleed air or electric mats, chemical fluid, pneumatic boots and mechanical expulsion.

chapters.example: A 3 mm ice layer forms over 12 m² of wing leading edge. Volume = 0.003 × 12 = 0.036 m³. With ice density 900 kg/m³, mass = 0.036 × 900 = 32.4 kg on one wing, before counting the loss of lift from the rough surface.
chapters.trap: Mixing anti-icing with de-icing, and forgetting the tailplane, pitot heads and engine inlets.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for the bleed air used for heating.
chapters.leave: Ice detector signals to Unit 3 or Unit 4; wiper motors to Unit 3.

links: hydraulic pressure retracts the gear and applies the brakes
bleed air drives the air turbine starter
bleed air feeds the pressurisation and cooling packs
fuel is metered and lit once the starter has spun the engine
air cycle for flight, vapour cycle for ground cooling
a pressurisation failure is what makes oxygen necessary
hot bleed air keeps the wing leading edge clear
gear position feeds the control, warning and interlock logic
